summary: Add the required incline force diagram, broaden exam practice across all four outcomes, and make impulse and changing-force methods explicit.

improvements.where: note, after the inclined-plane paragraph in ## Key ideas
improvements.why: The M1-4.2 syllabus point calls for motion on smooth or rough inclined planes, and the figure gate specifically requires a free_body diagram.
improvements.what: Add a free_body diagram of a particle on an inclined plane, showing weight $mg$ vertically downward, normal reaction $R$ perpendicular to the plane, and friction $F$ opposing an explicitly stated upward motion. In the adjacent note text, explain the resolved components $mg\sin\theta$ down the plane and $mg\cos\theta$ into it; do not put the resolved components on the same force diagram as extra forces. Embed the requested SVG in the note.

improvements.why: Only three items exist; none gives multi-phase motion or a rough incline, both explicit syllabus cases.
improvements.what: Add one structured exam item in which a connected particle hits the ground and the other continues in a new phase, and one rough-incline calculation requiring a correctly directed friction force and separate parallel/perpendicular equations.

improvements.why: Only three items exist, with no exam-style collision item or reversal-sign distractor.
improvements.what: Add a multi-part direct-collision question using signed momentum and final direction, plus a misconception MCQ about impulse for a particle reversing velocity.

improvements.why: The current set has no question resolving a resultant force into both $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ components or checking Newton's third-law bodies.
improvements.what: Add one vector $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$ calculation with two components and one conceptual MCQ distinguishing a third-law pair from forces on one body.

improvements.why: Only three items exist and the note's direction rule needs application when motion reverses or an applied force is oblique.
improvements.what: Add one rough-plane calculation that resolves an oblique applied force before finding $R$ and $F=\mu R$, plus one misconception MCQ about the direction of friction for a sliding particle. Keep within the M1 moving-friction scope.

improvements.why: The note states $J=\Delta p$ but omits $J=Ft$ for constant force and the impulse unit. The learner's M1 notes explain both on p.3.
improvements.what: Add the constant-force relation $J=Ft=m(v-u)$, with $\mathrm{N\,s}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, and a short signed-force or reversal example. Paraphrase the source.

improvements.where: note, after the connected-particles worked example
improvements.why: The method says to split phases when a particle hits the ground but never demonstrates the transition. Pearson explicitly includes a force changing after ground contact.
improvements.what: Add a concise two-phase worked example: find speed at contact, identify when the string slackens, then solve the remaining particle's motion with the new force balance. State why the old tension equation no longer applies.

improvements.why: The bundle lists a direct successor chapter on statics, but the note gives no Leads to link.
improvements.what: Append Leads to [[5 Statics of a particle]] using the bundle's exact note name.
